lead: Trigonometric levelling finds a height from a vertical angle and a horizontal distance, instead of from staff readings. It reaches points a level cannot: the top of a chimney or a temple tower, a hill station across a valley, or a pier in a river. When the base of the object can be reached, one angle and a taped distance do it. When it cannot, two instrument stations and a measured base give the distance as well. Few syllabi list it by name.
prereq: You need: vertical angles on both faces from Measurement of horizontal and vertical angles, and reduced levels, benchmarks and the curvature and refraction correction from levelling.

blocks.text: Set the theodolite at a station P, a horizontal distance D from the foot of the object, and sight its top T with a vertical angle α. The height of T above the instrument's horizontal axis is D tan α. To tie it to the datum, take a staff reading on a benchmark with the telescope horizontal: the RL of the instrument axis (its height of collimation) is RL of BM + that reading.
h = D tan α;   RL of T = RL of instrument axis + D tan α
blocks.where: D is the horizontal distance in metres (not the slope distance along the sight). α is positive for elevation and negative for depression. If the sight is taken to a target fixed a height t above the point wanted, subtract t.

blocks.text: For sights beyond about 300 m add the combined curvature and refraction correction, 0.0673 d² m with d in km, to the computed height (the earth falls away below the horizontal line of sight, so the point is higher than D tan α shows). At 165 m it is under 2 mm and is ignored.

sections.h3: Base inaccessible: stations in one vertical plane

blocks.text: When the foot of the object cannot be reached, D cannot be taped. Choose two stations P and Q on one straight line towards the object, with P nearer and Q a measured distance s farther away, so that P, Q and the top T lie in one vertical plane (the single plane method). Measure α₁ at P and α₂ at Q to T, and find the RL of the instrument axis at each station from a benchmark.

h₁ = D tan α₁ and h₂ = (D + s) tan α₂, with h₁ − h₂ = d
D = (s tan α₂ + d) ÷ (tan α₁ − tan α₂)
blocks.where: D is the horizontal distance from P to the vertical line through T. h₁ and h₂ are the heights of T above the instrument axis at P and at Q. d = (RL of axis at Q) − (RL of axis at P), positive when the axis at Q is higher. When both axes are at one level, d = 0 and D = s tan α₂ ÷ (tan α₁ − tan α₂).

blocks.text: The RL of T is found from P (axis RL + h₁) and checked from Q (axis RL + h₂). Because the equation forces the two answers to agree, this check catches arithmetic slips only; an error in s or in an angle passes unseen. So the base is taped twice and both angles are read on both faces.

sections.h3: Base inaccessible: stations not in one plane

blocks.text: Often no straight line towards the object is clear. In the double plane method P and Q are any two stations a measured distance s apart from which the top T is visible. At P measure the horizontal angle θ₁ between Q and T and the vertical angle α₁ to T; at Q measure θ₂ between P and T and α₂. The triangle PQT′ (T′ the point vertically below T) is solved in plan by the sine rule.

D<sub>P</sub> = s sin θ₂ ÷ sin(θ₁ + θ₂);   D<sub>Q</sub> = s sin θ₁ ÷ sin(θ₁ + θ₂)
RL of T = RL of axis at P + D<sub>P</sub> tan α₁ = RL of axis at Q + D<sub>Q</sub> tan α₂
blocks.where: D<sub>P</sub> and D<sub>Q</sub> are the horizontal distances from P and from Q to T′. θ₁ and θ₂ are the horizontal angles at P and Q inside triangle PQT′. The two RLs of T are computed separately; if they agree within the expected error, their mean is taken.

blocks.text: The angle at T′ is 180° − (θ₁ + θ₂); a very small angle there makes D sensitive to angle errors, so the stations are chosen to give a triangle with angles between about 30° and 120°.

examples.question: To find the RL of the top T of a water tower whose base is fenced off, stations P and Q are set out on a straight line towards it, Q being 60.000 m farther from the tower than P. A staff on a benchmark of RL 100.000 m reads 1.625 m with the telescope horizontal at P and 1.385 m at Q. The vertical angles to T are 12°30′ at P and 9°18′ at Q. Find the horizontal distance from P to the tower and the RL of T. Take tan 12°30′ = 0.22169 and tan 9°18′ = 0.16376.
steps: d = axis at Q − axis at P = 101.385 − 101.625 = −0.240 m (the axis at Q is lower).
Curvature and refraction at 0.165 km: 0.0673 × 0.165² = 0.002 m, negligible here.
examples.answer: The tower is 165.47 m from P, and its top is at RL 138.308 m (36.683 m above the axis at P).

examples.question: The same top is observed by the double plane method from two stations P and Q 80.000 m apart, not in line with the tower. At P the horizontal angle QPT′ is 62°00′ and the vertical angle to T is 18°30′00″; at Q the angle PQT′ is 54°00′ and the vertical angle is 17°12′20″. The axis RLs are 101.625 m at P and 101.385 m at Q. Find the RL of T from each station. Take sin 54° = 0.80902, sin 62° = 0.88295, sin 116° = 0.89879, tan 18°30′ = 0.33460 and tan 17°12′20″ = 0.30966.
steps: θ₁ + θ₂ = 62°00′ + 54°00′ = 116°00′; the angle at T′ is 64°00′, a well-shaped triangle.
The two differ by 2 mm, well within the reading accuracy, so the mean is taken: 125.720 m.
examples.answer: RL of T = 125.719 m from P and 125.721 m from Q; adopted value 125.720 m.

traps: Using the slope distance in D tan α. D is the horizontal distance; a taped or EDM slope distance is first reduced with cos α.
Forgetting the instrument axis. D tan α is the height above the axis, so the axis RL (benchmark RL + staff reading) is added.
Swapping the angles in the single plane formula. α₁ is from the nearer station P and is the larger angle; the formula gives D from P.
Getting the sign of d wrong. d is the axis RL at the far station minus that at the near station; here it was −0.240 m.
Using the opposite angle in the double plane method. D<sub>P</sub> uses sin θ₂, the angle at the other station.

quiz.q: When is the single plane method used and when the double plane method?
quiz.a: Single plane: when two stations can be set on one straight line towards the inaccessible object, so the stations and the object lie in one vertical plane. Double plane: when no such line is available and the two stations and the object form a triangle in plan.

quiz.q: Why is the height of the instrument axis found from a benchmark at each station?
quiz.a: D tan α gives the height of the point above the horizontal axis of the instrument at that station. To express it above the datum, the axis's own RL is needed, and it differs between stations because the ground and the tripod heights differ.

quiz.q: A chimney base is accessible and 120.000 m from the theodolite. The vertical angle to the top is 15°00′ and the axis RL is 98.450 m. Find the RL of the top. tan 15° = 0.26795.
In the single plane method s = 50.000 m, tan α₁ = 0.25000, tan α₂ = 0.20000 and both axes are at the same level. Find D from the nearer station and the height of the top above the axis.
In the double plane example, what happens to D<sub>P</sub> if the angle at T′ is only 10°, and why?
quiz.a: sin(θ₁ + θ₂) = sin 170° ≈ 0.174, a small divisor, so a few seconds of error in θ₁ or θ₂ change D<sub>P</sub> by a large fraction and the height becomes unreliable. The stations should be moved to give an angle of 30° or more at T′.

quiz.q: For a hill station 2.4 km across a valley, would you rely on trigonometric levelling from one end? Justify.
quiz.a: Not from one end alone. At 2.4 km the curvature and refraction correction is 0.0673 × 2.4² = 0.388 m, and refraction varies with the weather by a good part of that. Observations from both ends at the same time (reciprocal vertical angles) cancel curvature and most refraction, so they should be used.

beyond: Not for the exam. A total station measures the slope distance and the zenith angle together and computes the height difference at once, so trigonometric heighting is now routine over long sights. For control work, simultaneous reciprocal zenith angles cancel refraction. Search for reciprocal trigonometric levelling, refraction coefficient and total station height traversing.
